lessons.title: What a thru-hike is
lessons.objective: You can define thru-hike, section hike and Triple Crown.

payload.prompt: Which best describes a thru-hike?

options.text: Hiking a long trail from one end to the other in one continuous journey
options.explanation: That is the core idea: one trail, one end-to-end trip, usually over several months.

options.text: Hiking a whole trail in a single very long day
options.explanation: Covering a trail at record speed is a different pursuit, often called an FKT. A thru-hike is measured in months.

options.text: Any hike that returns you to your car
options.explanation: That describes a loop or an out-and-back. A thru-hike goes from one end of a trail to the other.

options.text: Sleeping in the same lodge every night and day-hiking from it
options.explanation: Staying in one base and day-hiking is not a thru-hike. Thru-hikers move their camp forward every day.

explanation.correct: A thru-hike means walking a long-distance trail end to end in one continuous push. It takes months, careful planning and a lot of patience.
explanation.incorrect: Think end to end: a thru-hiker starts at one terminus and walks to the other, camping and resupplying along the way, over months rather than days.
explanation.sayThisLine: "So you're thru-hiking the whole thing, start to finish?"

payload.prompt: Match each long-trail word to its meaning:

pairs.definition: Walking a long trail end to end in one continuous journey
Completing a long trail in pieces over weeks, months or years
Completing the Appalachian, Pacific Crest and Continental Divide Trails
One of the two ends of a long trail

explanation.summary: A thru-hike is one continuous trip, a section hike stitches pieces together, and the Triple Crown is the three famous American trails. Every long trail has two termini.
explanation.sayThisLine: "I've section hiked about half of it, a few weeks at a time."

payload.prompt: She finished a long trail over six summers, one piece at a time. A thru-hiker?

scene.alt: A hiker at a trail sign holding a map with several stretches of a long trail highlighted in different colors.

explanation.correct: Finishing a trail in pieces is a section hike. It is a real achievement, and many people complete long trails this way because of jobs, family and seasons.
explanation.incorrect: A thru-hike is one continuous journey. Completing a trail piece by piece over several years is a section hike, and it is every bit as valid, just a different rhythm.
explanation.sayThisLine: "Six summers of sections? That's a huge commitment."

payload.ruleTag: Continuous means thru, pieces mean section

payload.prompt: Finish the sentence about the Triple Crown:
payload.template: The Triple Crown is the {{first}} Trail, the Pacific Crest Trail and the {{third}} Trail.

explanation.correct: The American Triple Crown is the Appalachian Trail, the Pacific Crest Trail and the Continental Divide Trail. Each one is a multi-month walk on its own.
explanation.incorrect: The three trails are the Appalachian, the Pacific Crest and the Continental Divide. Between them they run down the east side, the west coast ranges and the spine of the Rockies.
explanation.sayThisLine: "He's done the AT and the PCT. He just needs the CDT for the Triple Crown."

statement.speaker: She
statement.text: I've been saving vacation for years. Next spring I'm taking leave to thru-hike, and I'm nervous and thrilled.

payload.question: What is she telling you?

options.text: She is planning a months-long end-to-end trail trip and it means a lot to her
options.explanation: Yes. Saving leave for a thru-hike shows how big a commitment it is, and she is sharing something personal.

options.text: She is planning a fun weekend loop
options.explanation: Years of saved leave point to a much bigger trip than a weekend loop.

options.text: She is planning to hike a trail in tiny pieces over years
options.explanation: That would be a section hike. She said she is taking leave for one continuous trip.

options.text: She is entering a speed race
options.explanation: Nothing in her words is about speed or records. She is talking about time away and nerves.

payload.translation: She has been planning a big, continuous long-trail trip for a long time, and she is both excited and a little scared.

followUps.line: Which trail are you thinking of?
followUps.why: A simple, curious question that lets her tell her story.

followUps.line: What are you most nervous about?
followUps.why: It gives room for the honest side of her excitement without you rushing to fix anything.

lessons.title: The big three trails
lessons.objective: You can place the AT, PCT and CDT and their rough lengths.

payload.prompt: About how long is the Appalachian Trail, Georgia to Maine?

explanation.correct: The AT is roughly 2,190 miles through 14 states, running from Georgia to Maine. The exact figure shifts a little when the route is rerouted.
explanation.incorrect: The Appalachian Trail is roughly 2,190 miles, Georgia to Maine, across 14 states. Official mileage changes slightly as sections are rerouted.
explanation.sayThisLine: "The AT is about twenty-two hundred miles, right?"

payload.prompt: About how long is the Pacific Crest Trail, Mexico to Canada?

explanation.correct: The PCT is roughly 2,650 miles, running through California, Oregon and Washington from the Mexican border to the Canadian border.
explanation.incorrect: The Pacific Crest Trail is roughly 2,650 miles, crossing California, Oregon and Washington from Mexico to Canada, through deserts, the Sierra Nevada and the Cascades.
explanation.sayThisLine: "The PCT runs about twenty-six hundred miles, border to border."

payload.prompt: Which description fits the Continental Divide Trail?

options.text: About 3,000 miles along the Rockies from Mexico to Canada, the longest of the three
options.explanation: Yes. The CDT follows the Continental Divide through New Mexico, Colorado, Wyoming, Idaho and Montana.

options.text: About 2,200 miles from Georgia to Maine through green eastern forest
options.explanation: That is the Appalachian Trail, not the Continental Divide Trail.

options.text: About 2,650 miles down the Sierra Nevada and Cascades
options.explanation: That describes the Pacific Crest Trail, which runs along the western mountain ranges.

options.text: A short 500-mile loop through the desert
options.explanation: The CDT is one of the longest trails in the country and it is not a loop.

explanation.correct: The CDT is roughly 3,000 miles from Mexico to Canada along the Continental Divide. Its route is less continuous and less marked than the AT or PCT, so hikers often do more navigating.
explanation.incorrect: Match each trail to its landscape: AT in the east, PCT along the western ranges, CDT along the Rockies and the Continental Divide, roughly 3,000 miles, Mexico to Canada.
explanation.sayThisLine: "The CDT is the longest and wildest of the three, isn't it?"

payload.prompt: She is a NOBO on the AT. Where does she start, and which way does she walk?

options.text: She starts in Georgia and walks north toward Maine
options.explanation: NOBO means northbound. On the AT that means Georgia to Maine, usually starting in spring as the weather warms.

options.text: She starts in Maine and walks south toward Georgia
options.explanation: That is a SOBO, a southbound hiker, not a NOBO.

options.text: She starts in the middle and hikes out and back
options.explanation: NOBO and SOBO describe direction, not a starting point in the middle.

options.text: NOBO means no bears on the trail
options.explanation: It is an abbreviation for northbound, not a wildlife term.

explanation.correct: NOBO is northbound and SOBO is southbound. On the AT, NOBOs typically start in Georgia in spring and follow the warm weather north.
explanation.incorrect: NOBO means northbound. On the Appalachian Trail that is Georgia toward Maine. A SOBO goes the other way, Maine toward Georgia.
explanation.sayThisLine: "I'm a NOBO. I start in Georgia in the spring."

payload.prompt: Match each trail to where it runs:

pairs.definition: Georgia to Maine through 14 eastern states
Mexican border to Canadian border via California, Oregon and Washington
Mexican border to Canadian border along the Rockies through five states
A hiker walking a long trail from north to south

explanation.summary: The AT is the eastern classic, the PCT follows the western ranges, and the CDT follows the Continental Divide. SOBO describes direction, and any of the three can be walked either way.
explanation.sayThisLine: "The AT runs through Georgia to Maine, and the PCT runs Mexico to Canada."

lessons.title: Trail names and tramilies
lessons.objective: You can explain trail names and tramilies.

statement.speaker: She
statement.text: My trail name is Biscuit. Someone gave it to me on day three after I ate a whole tray of them at a hostel.

payload.question: What is she sharing?

options.text: A trail nickname she was given, with the funny story behind it
options.explanation: Yes. Trail names are usually given by other hikers, often after something funny or memorable.

options.text: A brand of food she carries
options.explanation: Biscuit is her nickname, not a product. The tray of biscuits is the story of how she got it.

options.text: The name on her official permit
options.explanation: Permits use legal names. A trail name is an informal nickname among hikers.

options.text: The name of the trail she hiked
options.explanation: She is talking about herself, not the route.

payload.translation: On long trails, hikers get nicknames from the people they meet, and hers came from a funny moment on day three.

followUps.line: Biscuit! Do you still like biscuits after all that?
followUps.why: It is playful, shows you followed the story and lets her laugh at herself.

followUps.line: Do you have a favorite trail-name story from someone else?
followUps.why: It invites more stories and shows curiosity about the culture, not just about her.

payload.prompt: How do trail names traditionally come about?

options.text: Usually another hiker gives you one after something you said or did, and you decide whether to keep it
options.explanation: This is the common custom. A name that is earned tends to come with a story.

options.text: You should announce your own cool name on day one
options.explanation: Choosing your own is looked at with a smile by many, since the tradition leans toward being given one.

options.text: The trail organization assigns every hiker one at registration
options.explanation: No organization hands out trail names. They come from hikers and stay informal.

options.text: You must use it on your permit
options.explanation: Permits use legal names. Trail names are a social tradition.

explanation.correct: Trail names are traditionally given by fellow hikers, often from a funny moment, and the hiker chooses whether it sticks. Many people also use one just for fun, so there is room to be relaxed about it.
explanation.incorrect: The classic custom is that other hikers give you a trail name based on something you did, and you can keep it or not. It is an informal tradition, so no one hands them out officially.
explanation.sayThisLine: "Did you get your trail name, or did you pick your own?"

payload.prompt: She says her tramily kept her going. Are they her actual relatives?

scene.alt: A small group of hikers laughing together around a picnic table at a trail campsite at dusk.

explanation.correct: Tramily is short for trail family, the group of hikers who end up walking, camping and celebrating together on a long trail. They are friends made on the way.
explanation.incorrect: A tramily is a trail family: a group of hikers who bond over weeks on the trail. It says nothing about blood relatives.
explanation.sayThisLine: "Tell me about your tramily. Who were they?"

payload.title: Her trail name and her tramily
payload.setting: Chatting after she comes back from a month on a long trail

exchanges.theirMessage: They called me Sherpa out there, because I ended up carrying everyone's snacks. I loved it.

replies.text: Sherpa! That is a great trail name. Who came up with it?
replies.theirResponse: My tramily did, on a rainy afternoon. Someone said it, and it stuck.
replies.coachNote: You show you know names are given by others and ask for the story.

replies.text: Fun. So what's your real name again?
replies.theirResponse: Uh, the same one you've been using.
replies.coachNote: A trail name is part of her story. Ask about it before circling back.

replies.text: I'd pick something cooler than that for myself.
replies.theirResponse: Well, that is sort of the point. You don't pick it.
replies.coachNote: Names are given, not chosen. Do not put down her nickname.

exchanges.theirMessage: Honestly the hardest part was saying goodbye to my tramily when I went home.

replies.text: That sounds hard. Are you still in touch with them?
replies.theirResponse: Yes, we have a group chat. We're already planning a reunion hike.
replies.coachNote: You acknowledged the feeling and asked something gentle.

replies.text: They were just people you met, right?
replies.theirResponse: Not really. After weeks together they felt like family.
replies.coachNote: You missed why tramily is a word at all. Ask, do not minimize.

replies.text: I can imagine. What was your favorite tramily moment?
replies.theirResponse: Cooking terrible dinner together on a windy ridge. Best night ever.
replies.coachNote: A warm, curious question that lets her relive it.

payload.closingNote: Trail names and tramilies are the social heart of long-trail life. Listening for the story is what makes you good company.

statement.speaker: He
statement.text: We started as strangers, but by week three my tramily and I were sharing every campsite and cooking together.

payload.question: What is he describing?

options.text: A group of hikers who bonded and started traveling together
options.explanation: Yes. That is what a tramily is: a trail family formed through days of shared miles.

options.text: A commercial guided tour
options.explanation: He said they started as strangers and bonded on their own. Nobody guided them.

options.text: A shared resupply box
options.explanation: He mentioned sharing campsites and cooking, not mailing supplies.

options.text: A rest day in town
options.explanation: A rest day is a zero. He described a group that stays together over weeks.

payload.translation: He met other hikers, and over a few weeks they became close friends who camp and cook together like a family.

followUps.line: How did you all end up hiking together?
followUps.why: It invites the origin story, which is the heart of every tramily.
A light, curious question that shows you picked up on the cooking detail.

lessons.title: Trail magic, hiker hunger
lessons.objective: You can recognize trail magic and hiker hunger stories.

statement.speaker: She
statement.text: I came down to the road at the end of a brutal day and there was a cooler of cold sodas and a guy grilling hot dogs. Total trail magic.

payload.question: What just happened to her?

options.text: Someone offered hikers free food and drink as a kindness
options.explanation: Yes. Free food, a ride or a place to rest offered to hikers is trail magic.

options.text: She bought lunch at a roadside stand
options.explanation: The point is that it was free and unexpected, not a purchase.

options.text: She was rescued from an emergency
options.explanation: It was a happy surprise at the end of a hard day, not an emergency.

options.text: She joined a paid guided trip
options.explanation: Nothing she said involves a tour or a payment.

payload.translation: A stranger set up free food and drinks for hikers at the road crossing, and it made her day.

followUps.line: Did you get to thank whoever was grilling?
followUps.why: Thanking trail angels is part of the culture, and it shows warmth.

followUps.line: What was the best trail magic you ever got?
followUps.why: Everyone has a favorite trail-magic story, and it is an easy way to keep her talking.

payload.prompt: Finish the trail magic etiquette:
payload.template: Say {{thanks}} to the trail angels, take only {{amount}} so there is enough for the hikers behind you, and pack out your trash.

explanation.correct: Trail angels give freely, so the polite response is thanks, a fair share and no litter. Leaving the spot clean also helps them keep doing it.
explanation.incorrect: Say thank you, take only your fair share so others can enjoy it too, and carry out your trash. Kindness stays on the trail when hikers respect it.
explanation.sayThisLine: "Thank you so much. I'll take one and leave plenty for the next hikers."

payload.prompt: A thru-hiker in town orders two entrees and dessert, then more. What is going on?

options.text: Hiker hunger: weeks of long days burn so many calories that appetite becomes enormous
options.explanation: Yes. Many thru-hikers describe a huge appetite that shows up after weeks of daily long-distance hiking.

options.text: She is showing off for the table
options.explanation: The hunger is real. Long trail days use far more energy than everyday life.

options.text: It is always a sign that she is sick
options.explanation: A big appetite after long hiking days is normal. It is not by itself a sign of illness.

options.text: She has been carrying too little food
options.explanation: This may play a part, but the hunger is mostly the body catching up on weeks of high energy use.

explanation.correct: After weeks of daily long hiking, the body demands a lot of fuel. Hiker hunger is a well-known part of thru-hiking, and town meals often get very large.
explanation.incorrect: Hiker hunger is the huge appetite thru-hikers develop after weeks of long days. It is a normal result of high energy use, and it is why town meals get big.
explanation.sayThisLine: "Hiker hunger hit and I ate two pizzas."

payload.prompt: You find a cooler by the road with a note: help yourself. Take the whole thing?

scene.alt: A cooler and a folding table of snacks at a trailhead road crossing, with a hand-written sign inviting hikers to help themselves.

choices.label: Take a little, leave the rest

explanation.correct: Trail magic is a gift to everyone who comes after you. Taking a fair share, thanking whoever set it up and leaving the spot tidy keeps the tradition alive.
explanation.incorrect: Emptying a shared cooler leaves nothing for hikers behind you. Take a fair share, leave the rest and clean up after yourself.
explanation.sayThisLine: "I'll take one, and leave the rest for the next hikers."

payload.ruleTag: Fair share, then leave it tidy

payload.prompt: Complete the sentence about long-trail appetite:
payload.template: After weeks of long days, hikers burn far {{more}} energy than at home, so they eat {{often}} and their town meals are huge.

explanation.correct: Steady hiking day after day burns far more energy than an ordinary day, so thru-hikers eat often on trail, and their appetite in town can be enormous.
explanation.incorrect: Long trail days burn far more energy than normal. Hikers eat often on trail, and after weeks of it they arrive in town extremely hungry.
explanation.sayThisLine: "You must be starving. Let's get you a real meal."

lessons.title: Zeros, neros, resupply
lessons.objective: You can follow a thru-hiker's logistics talk.

payload.prompt: Match each logistics word to what it means:

pairs.definition: A rest day with no trail miles
A near-zero day with only a few miles
Buying or collecting food and supplies for the next stretch
A free box where hikers leave and take extra food and gear

explanation.summary: Zeros and neros are rest days in town, resupply is restocking food for the next stretch, and hiker boxes are a way to share leftovers.
explanation.sayThisLine: "I'm taking a zero in town, then resupplying for the next four days."

payload.prompt: The next town is five days away. How much food do you buy?

situation.narrative: You are planning a resupply on a long trail. The next town with a store is about five days of hiking ahead. Trail magic is not guaranteed, and the food you carry is your safety margin.

options.label: Buy five days of food plus a spare day of easy snacks
options.consequence: A small cushion covers a slow day, a detour or a weather delay. It costs a little weight and buys a lot of peace of mind.
considerations: Delays are common, so extra food is part of the plan.
Bring food that is easy to eat when you are tired.

options.label: Buy exactly five days of food and no more
options.consequence: This works if nothing goes wrong, but there is no cushion for a delay, a detour or an injury.
considerations: Little margin means a small problem becomes a big one.
Consider a spare day of snacks.

options.label: Buy three days of food and count on trail magic
options.consequence: Trail magic is a gift, not a plan. Running short of food between towns is a real risk.
considerations: Never plan meals around kindness that might not appear.
Hunger lowers judgment and energy.

options.label: Buy little and plan to hitchhike to a store whenever needed
options.consequence: Roads can be far away and traffic scarce. Do not count on an easy ride or a nearby shop.
considerations: Check the guidebook for real access points.
Carry your own food first.

payload.expertNote: Experienced long-distance hikers count days between resupply points, add a small buffer and keep an eye on the forecast before leaving town.
payload.sayThisLine: "Five days to the next town, so I'm packing six days of food."
payload.safetyNote: Check current guidebooks, trail reports and land manager guidance for real resupply options. Follow food storage rules for the area, such as bear canisters where required.

payload.prompt: Why do thru-hikers take zero days?

options.text: To rest their bodies, do laundry, resupply and eat real food in town
options.explanation: Yes. A zero is a recovery and logistics day, and it is part of a sustainable long-trail pace.

options.text: To gain an advantage over other hikers in a race
options.explanation: Thru-hiking is not a race for most people, and rest days help rather than hurt.

options.text: Because the rules require a rest day each week
options.explanation: No rule requires it. Hikers choose when to rest.

options.text: To wait until the trail is empty
options.explanation: The point is recovery and logistics, not avoiding people.

explanation.correct: A zero day gives tired legs a break and lets hikers do laundry, shower, shop and eat. It is a normal, healthy part of long-trail life.
explanation.incorrect: Zeros are for recovery and errands: rest, laundry, food and repairs. They are not a rule or a race tactic.
explanation.sayThisLine: "I'm taking a zero in town to rest my feet."

payload.prompt: Put a sensible town resupply day in order:

items.text: Check in with your contact and check the forecast for the next stretch
items.why: Letting someone know you are safe and seeing the weather ahead shapes every other choice.

items.text: Shower, do laundry and eat a real meal
items.why: Recovering your body and morale makes the next stretch easier.

items.text: Count the days to the next town and plan meals with a spare day
items.why: Working out how much you need before shopping prevents buying too little.

items.text: Shop for food and check gear for repairs
items.why: Shopping after you have a plan avoids overbuying or missing something important.

items.text: Repack your food and store it as the area requires
items.why: Packing food properly protects it and the wildlife around your camps.

explanation.correct: Check in and forecast, recover, plan the days, shop and repair, then pack food safely. Each step sets up the next.
explanation.incorrect: Start with check-in and the forecast, recover, plan the days you need, shop, then repack and store food properly for the next stretch.
explanation.sayThisLine: "Check in, rest, plan, shop, pack. Then I'm back on trail."

payload.prompt: Complete the rest-day words:
payload.template: A {{zero}} day has no trail miles, and a {{nero}} day has just a few.

explanation.correct: A zero is no miles at all, and a nero is nearly zero, like walking a few miles into town. Both give hikers time to recover.
explanation.incorrect: Zero means zero miles hiked. Nero is a near-zero day with only a few miles, often into or out of town.
explanation.sayThisLine: "I'm doing a nero, four easy miles into town, then a full zero tomorrow."

lessons.title: Peakbagging lists
lessons.objective: You can explain why people chase lists like 14ers and the Adirondack 46.

payload.prompt: Why do so many people chase peak lists?

options.text: A list turns a region into a series of goals, gives a sense of progress and brings people to places they would not otherwise visit
options.explanation: Lists add structure, milestones and a reason to explore. Many peakbaggers say the community is part of the appeal.

options.text: Because land managers require everyone to complete a list
options.explanation: No agency requires list-chasing. It is a voluntary hobby.

options.text: Because it is the cheapest way to hike
options.explanation: Lists are about motivation and goals, not cost.

options.text: Because every peak on the lists is an easy walk
options.explanation: Peaks on lists vary from casual walks to serious climbs, so conditions and skill always matter.

explanation.correct: Lists give structure and milestones, and they lead hikers to new places and new friends. It is a voluntary hobby, and the rules of each list are set by the people who care about it.
explanation.incorrect: Peakbagging is a voluntary hobby. People like the goal, the progress and the community, not a requirement or a promise of easy summits.
explanation.sayThisLine: "I like having a list. It gets me to peaks I'd never think to visit."

statement.speaker: He
statement.text: I'm chasing the Colorado fourteeners. I've done nine, and next weekend I'm going for number ten if the weather holds.

payload.question: What is he doing?

options.text: Peakbagging: working through a list of peaks above 14,000 feet
options.explanation: Yes. Fourteeners are peaks over 14,000 feet, and many people work through them as a list.

options.text: Thru-hiking a long trail end to end
options.explanation: He is climbing separate peaks, not walking one continuous trail.

options.text: Staying in mountain huts
options.explanation: He did not mention huts or lodges.

options.text: Setting a speed record
options.explanation: There is no mention of speed or records. He mentions the count and the weather.

payload.translation: He is climbing Colorado's peaks above 14,000 feet one by one and is watching the weather before his next attempt.

followUps.line: Which one was your favorite so far?
followUps.why: It invites a personal story rather than a number.

followUps.line: Do you start before dawn to beat the afternoon storms?
followUps.why: It shows you know the alpine-start habit and respects his safety mindset.

payload.prompt: Clouds build at 11 AM. The summit is 40 minutes away and it would finish your list. Now what?

situation.narrative: You have worked on a peak list for two summers, and this is the last one. It is late morning, the summit is close, and thunderheads are stacking over the neighboring ridge. Your friend is eager to finish.

options.label: Turn around now and come back another day
options.consequence: The peak will still be there. Being off exposed ground before the storm is worth far more than a checkmark on a list.
considerations: A list is a hobby, not a deadline.
Building clouds at 11 AM can become storms before noon.

options.label: Wait below the exposed section for 15 minutes with a firm turn-back rule
options.consequence: A short, disciplined wait can be reasonable if you set the rule first and stay out of exposed terrain. Turn back if the clouds keep growing.
considerations: Agree on the rule before you wait.
Do not drift up because it looks a little better.

options.label: Rush up and back quickly to beat the storm
options.consequence: Speed does not protect you from lightning. You would be on the highest point when storms are likely.
considerations: Summit fever pushes people to take risks they would not otherwise accept.
Hurrying on rocky ground invites falls.

options.label: Send the fastest hiker up while the others wait
options.consequence: That puts one person alone on exposed ground with no help nearby.
considerations: Groups make decisions together and stay together.
The list is not worth a solo risk.

payload.expertNote: Peakbaggers who last are the ones who turn around. Most of them will tell you a list is finished one safe trip at a time.
payload.sayThisLine: "The list can wait. Let's get down before those clouds turn."
payload.safetyNote: Check the mountain forecast, start early and follow land manager guidance. No list is worth a lightning risk.

payload.prompt: She is working on the Adirondack 46. Is that a list of peaks or one long trail?

scene.alt: A hiker on a rocky summit in a forested mountain range, with rolling peaks stretching out in every direction.

explanation.correct: The Adirondack 46 is a list of high peaks in New York's Adirondack Mountains. People climb them one by one, on separate trips, rather than along a single trail.
explanation.incorrect: The Adirondack 46 is a list of high peaks in New York, not a single trail. Hikers tick them off over many trips.
explanation.sayThisLine: "How many of the forty-six have you done?"

payload.ruleTag: Peak lists are collections, not routes

payload.prompt: Finish the list-chaser's safety rule:
payload.template: The {{list}} is a hobby, so if weather turns or someone is unwell, {{turn}} and come back another day.

explanation.correct: A peak list is a voluntary hobby, so it never outranks safety. When weather turns or someone struggles, turning around is the smart move and the peak will wait.
explanation.incorrect: A list is a hobby, not an obligation. Turn around when weather or health says so, because the mountain will still be there another day.
explanation.sayThisLine: "It's just a list. We'll come back."

lessons.title: How wilderness got protected
lessons.objective: You can outline the Wilderness Act and how it shapes hiking.

payload.prompt: Put these public-lands milestones in order, earliest first:

items.text: 1872: Yellowstone is set aside as the first U.S. national park
items.why: Yellowstone came first and started the idea of national parks in the United States.

items.text: 1906: The Antiquities Act lets presidents protect sites as national monuments
items.why: It gave presidents a tool to protect places without waiting for new park laws.

items.text: 1916: Congress creates the National Park Service
items.why: One agency was created to manage the parks and to protect them for future generations.

items.text: 1964: The Wilderness Act creates the National Wilderness Preservation System
items.why: It set up a system of designated wilderness with strong limits on motors and structures.

items.text: 1968: The National Trails System Act names the first national scenic trails
items.why: It recognized the Appalachian and Pacific Crest Trails as the first national scenic trails.

explanation.correct: Yellowstone in 1872, the Antiquities Act in 1906, the National Park Service in 1916, the Wilderness Act in 1964 and the National Trails System Act in 1968.
explanation.incorrect: The order is 1872 Yellowstone, 1906 Antiquities Act, 1916 National Park Service, 1964 Wilderness Act, 1968 National Trails System Act.
explanation.sayThisLine: "The Park Service came in 1916, and the Wilderness Act followed in 1964."

payload.prompt: You are hiking in a designated wilderness area. What does the Wilderness Act mean for you?

options.text: No motor vehicles or bikes, and no permanent roads or buildings, with rules set by the managing agency
options.explanation: This is the heart of the Act. Wilderness is meant to stay free of motors, mechanical transport and permanent structures.

options.text: Bikes are fine because they have no motor
options.explanation: Mechanical transport such as bicycles is generally not allowed in designated wilderness.

options.text: Nobody may enter at all
options.explanation: Wilderness is open to foot and horse travel. It is protected, not closed.

options.text: Roads and lodges will be built for visitor comfort
options.explanation: The opposite is true. Wilderness keeps out roads and permanent structures.

explanation.correct: The 1964 Wilderness Act limits motors, mechanical transport, permanent roads and structures in designated wilderness. Hikers can walk in, but should always check the managing agency's rules and permit requirements.
explanation.incorrect: Designated wilderness is protected from motors, bikes, roads and buildings. Foot and horse travel are how you see it, and each area has its own rules and permits.
explanation.sayThisLine: "It's designated wilderness, so no bikes and no motors."

payload.prompt: The Wilderness Act calls wilderness land 'untrammeled by man.' How should you think about that?

options.text: These lands have long been homelands of Native peoples, who lived on, traveled through and cared for them, and who are still here
options.explanation: This is accurate. The law's language describes how land is managed today, but it does not mean nobody ever lived there.

options.text: The lands were empty until explorers arrived
options.explanation: That is inaccurate. Indigenous peoples lived on and cared for these lands for thousands of years.

options.text: Native peoples left long ago and no longer have any connection to the land
options.explanation: Native nations are still here today, and many have living ties to these places.

options.text: It is best not to bring up history when hiking
options.explanation: Learning whose land you are on is part of respectful hiking. Silence hides the fuller story.

explanation.correct: The phrase describes how the law manages land, not the whole story. Native nations lived on, traveled through and stewarded these lands long before parks and wilderness areas existed, and they are still here.
explanation.incorrect: Wilderness was never empty. Native peoples have long homelands across these places, and many national parks were created in ways that displaced or excluded Native people. Learn whose land you are on.
explanation.sayThisLine: "I try to learn whose homelands I'm hiking on."

statement.speaker: She
statement.text: Before we start, I like to look up whose homelands a trail crosses. Today it's the ancestral lands of a Native nation still living here, and I'd like to learn more.

payload.question: What is she doing?

options.text: Learning whose land she is on and showing respect by wanting to know more
options.explanation: Yes. Looking up the Native nation's own information, and staying curious, is a respectful habit.

options.text: Starting an argument before the hike
options.explanation: She is sharing a personal habit, not picking a fight.

options.text: Saying the history is over and done
options.explanation: She said the nation is still living here, so the connection is current.

options.text: Reading permit rules aloud
options.explanation: Nothing she said is about permits.

payload.translation: She likes to learn about the Native nation whose homelands the trail crosses, and she treats that as a living connection, not just history.

followUps.line: Where do you look that up?
followUps.why: It is sincere, and it invites her to share good sources, like a tribe's own website.

followUps.line: What did you learn about this place today?
followUps.why: It keeps the conversation about learning rather than performing.

payload.prompt: A trailhead sign honors the Native nations of this land. Your date shrugs: 'Just words.' What do you say?

situation.narrative: At a trailhead, a sign names the Native nation or nations whose homelands you are entering. Your date is skeptical. You would like to respond honestly without lecturing, and without claiming knowledge you do not have.

facts.label: Sign says
facts.value: Names the nation whose homelands these are

options.label: Say it is a start, and you want to learn more from the nation's own website
options.consequence: You stay honest about what you know, agree that words alone are not enough and turn the moment into curiosity and action.
considerations: Naming the nation matters most when it leads to learning.
A tribe's own website is a better source than a guess.

options.label: Listen, say you are not sure, and look it up together later
options.consequence: Admitting what you do not know is honest, and following up keeps the door open.
considerations: Follow through on the promise to look it up.
Curiosity is more respectful than pretending.

options.label: Agree it is just for show and skip the sign
options.consequence: You miss the chance to learn whose land this is, and you brush off a real, living connection.
considerations: Native nations are still here.
Dismissing the sign does not help anyone.

options.label: Claim a distant Native ancestor to sound authoritative
options.consequence: Claiming heritage you cannot back up is disrespectful and can hurt real Native people.
considerations: Speak from what you truly know.
Let Native voices speak for themselves.

payload.expertNote: A land acknowledgement is strongest when it is specific, accurate and followed by something real: learning from the nation itself, respecting closures for cultural sites and supporting Native-led conservation.
payload.sayThisLine: "It's a start. I'd like to learn who's here and what they'd want hikers to know."
payload.safetyNote: Respect posted closures and cultural-site rules, which protect places that matter to Native nations. Follow land manager guidance.

lessons.title: Hut-to-hut and classic walks
lessons.objective: You can describe hut-to-hut trekking and famous long walks.

payload.prompt: What is hut-to-hut hiking?

options.text: Walking a route and sleeping each night in mountain huts or lodges, often with meals, so you carry less
options.explanation: Yes. Huts give you a bed and often food, so you can carry a lighter pack than on a camping trip.

options.text: Carrying a tent and camping wherever you like
options.explanation: That is backpacking with a tent. Hut-to-hut uses existing lodges.

options.text: Staying in a single hut and never moving
options.explanation: Hut-to-hut means moving between huts along a route.

options.text: Showing up anywhere with no plan or booking
options.explanation: Popular huts often need reservations, so planning ahead matters.

explanation.correct: Hut-to-hut trekking links mountain huts or refuges along a route. Many offer beds and meals, and popular ones fill up, so booking ahead is part of the plan.
explanation.incorrect: Hut-to-hut means walking between huts, not camping. You sleep and often eat at the huts, and you usually need reservations for popular routes.
explanation.sayThisLine: "We're doing a hut-to-hut in the Alps, so no tent this time."

statement.speaker: He
statement.text: We did the Tour du Mont Blanc last summer. About a week, a new refuge every night, and we crossed through France, Italy and Switzerland.

payload.question: What kind of trip is he describing?

options.text: A hut-to-hut trek around a big mountain, sleeping in refuges
options.explanation: Yes. The Tour du Mont Blanc loops around Mont Blanc and is a classic hut-to-hut route.

options.text: A months-long thru-hike of a national trail
options.explanation: He described about a week and a new refuge each night, not months on a single trail.

options.text: A peakbagging list
options.explanation: He did not mention summits or lists, only refuges and crossing borders.

options.text: A camping trip with a tent
options.explanation: He said a new refuge every night, which means lodges, not a tent.

payload.translation: He walked a loop around Mont Blanc over about a week, staying in a mountain refuge each night and crossing three countries.

followUps.line: Did you have to book the refuges way ahead?
followUps.why: It shows you know popular huts often need reservations.

followUps.line: What was the best view of the trip?
followUps.why: A warm, open question that lets him share what he loved.

payload.prompt: About how long is the Tour du Mont Blanc loop?

explanation.correct: The Tour du Mont Blanc is roughly 105 miles, or about 170 kilometers, and hikers commonly take about a week or more to finish it.
explanation.incorrect: The Tour du Mont Blanc loop is roughly 105 miles, about 170 kilometers, through France, Italy and Switzerland. Most hikers take about a week or more.
explanation.sayThisLine: "It's about a hundred miles around the mountain, and worth every step."

payload.prompt: Match each classic walk to what it is known for:

pairs.definition: A hut-to-hut loop around Mont Blanc through France, Italy and Switzerland
A network of historic pilgrimage routes across Spain and beyond
A roughly 210-mile trail through California's Sierra Nevada
Mountain huts run by the Appalachian Mountain Club in New Hampshire's White Mountains

explanation.summary: These are some of the best-known long walks. Some are hut-to-hut, some are pilgrimages and some are wilderness trails, so check each one's rules and booking needs.
explanation.sayThisLine: "I'd love to walk the Camino someday, or the Tour du Mont Blanc."

payload.prompt: You plan a popular hut route in summer. Book beds ahead?

scene.alt: A stone mountain hut at dusk with lit windows, and a line of hikers arriving along the trail.

explanation.correct: Popular huts can fill up in summer, and arriving with no bed can leave you tired and stuck. Book ahead and check each hut's cancellation and arrival rules.
explanation.incorrect: Huts have limited beds and the popular ones sell out. Booking ahead protects your plan and your safety at the end of a long day.
explanation.sayThisLine: "We booked every hut ahead. Summer beds fill up fast."
